d.title: Where would this value go? Answered for a whole array at once
d.caption: **One primitive replaces a surprising number of loops**, because “which bucket does each of these million values fall into” is the same question as “where would each one be inserted”. The `side` argument is the whole specification at a boundary: left puts an exact match before the equal element, right puts it after — which is the difference between a half-open bucket and a closed one. **And the warning in the last row is unconditional: the array must be sorted, searchsorted does not check, and on unsorted input it returns a confident, meaningless answer.**

d.title: Two rules, and every one of these follows from them
d.caption: **Rule one: a letter repeated across the inputs is summed over. Rule two: a letter absent from the output is summed over.** That is the entire notation, and the table is just those two rules applied. Once they are internalised, `einsum` stops being cryptic and starts being the shortest way to say what you mean — particularly for batched and contracted operations that have no NumPy function of their own. **The one to read twice is the trace: `ii` repeats the letter *and* omits it from the output, so both rules fire at once.**

state: i repeated, kept in the output

d.title: Four decompositions, and the one that finds a dependency you did not know about
d.caption: **The SVD row is the practically important one: singular values come out sorted, so a near-zero one is a column that is almost a combination of the others.** Here the fourth is about 1e-8 and the rank comes back as 9 rather than 10 — a duplicate feature found without looking for it. **And PCA is not a separate algorithm: it is the SVD of centred data**, which is worth knowing because it explains every property PCA has. The last row is the cheap habit: `eigh` on a symmetric matrix is faster than `eig`, guarantees real eigenvalues, and returns them sorted.

d.title: NumPy's answer to missing data, and why pandas went elsewhere
d.caption: **A masked array keeps the data and a separate boolean array of what is invalid, and every operation respects the mask** — which is genuinely the right model, and is also why pandas did not adopt it. The mask has to be propagated through every function, so anything that leaves the masked-array world loses it, and the performance cost is paid on every operation whether or not anything is missing. **Know it exists, recognise it in older scientific code, and reach for NaN or a nullable dtype instead** — then `filled(np.nan)` is how you get back out.

d.title: diff comes back one element shorter, which is what makes it awkward as a feature
d.caption: **A difference of n values has n−1 answers, so the result no longer lines up with the index it came from** — and a feature that silently shifts by one row is a bug that produces plausible numbers. `prepend` fixes the alignment explicitly. **`gradient` solves it differently, with central differences: same length, and more accurate in the interior** because it looks both ways rather than backwards only. For a time series where the spacing is uneven, pass the coordinate array and it uses the real spacing instead of assuming 1.

d.title: Two polynomial APIs that order their coefficients opposite ways
d.caption: **The modern class returns coefficients low-order first and the legacy function returns them high-order first, and nothing warns you** — so a fit that is read with the wrong convention produces a curve that is wrong in a way that still looks like a curve. Prefer the class: it also rescales the input domain internally, which is the reason its fit is better conditioned at higher degrees. **And the degree is the real decision, not the API:** raising it always reduces the training error and starts tracking the noise instead of the signal.
